identity.title: Robot Dynamics (Newton-Euler / Lagrangian)
identity.tagline: Moving beyond 'where is it' to 'how much torque does it actually take to move it there.'

simpleSummary: The study of how much force or torque is actually needed to make a robot move the way you want, accounting for its mass, inertia, and gravity — not just describing the motion itself.
keyIdea: Robot dynamics relates joint torques and forces to the resulting motion (and vice versa), accounting for mass, inertia, gravity, and velocity-dependent coupling effects between joints — computed via one of two classical, mathematically equivalent methods.
overview: Kinematics (forward, inverse, and velocity kinematics) describes a robot's motion purely geometrically — positions, orientations, and velocities — without any reference to what forces or torques are actually needed to produce that motion. Dynamics fills in that missing piece: it relates the torques a robot's motors apply to the resulting joint accelerations, accounting for every link's mass and inertia, gravity acting on the whole structure, and the way a moving arm's own joints dynamically interact with each other. This matters immensely in practice: correctly sizing a robot arm's motors requires knowing the actual worst-case torque needed at each joint, and any model-based controller more sophisticated than basic PID (like feedforward gravity compensation, or Model Predictive Control) needs an accurate dynamics model to work well.

equations.label: General Manipulator Dynamics Equation
equations.meaning: τ is the vector of joint torques; q, q̇, q̈ are joint positions, velocities, and accelerations; M(q) is the configuration-dependent mass/inertia matrix; C(q,q̇)q̇ captures velocity-dependent Coriolis and centrifugal coupling between joints; G(q) is the configuration-dependent gravity torque.

equations.label: Simple 1-Link Pendulum Example
equations.meaning: For a single arm of mass m and length L at angle θ from horizontal, this gives the joint torque needed: the first term accelerates the arm, the second (m·g·L·cos θ) is exactly the gravity-compensation torque needed just to hold the arm still at that angle.

howItWorks: Two classical methods derive the same underlying equations of motion. The Newton-Euler approach works link by link: a forward pass propagates velocities and accelerations from the base out to the tip, then a backward pass propagates forces and torques from the tip back to the base, applying Newton's second law (force = mass × acceleration) and its rotational equivalent at each link. This recursive structure is computationally efficient, which is why it's the method typically used inside real-time robot control software. The Lagrangian approach instead starts from the whole system's total kinetic and potential energy and applies the Euler-Lagrange equation to derive the equations of motion symbolically — a more systematic and often more intuitive method for deriving dynamics by hand or in symbolic math software, though less computationally efficient for real-time recursive evaluation on arms with many links. Both methods produce the identical τ = M(q)q̈ + C(q,q̇)q̇ + G(q) structure: M(q) is the effective mass/inertia 'felt' at each joint, which genuinely changes with the arm's configuration (an outstretched arm has more effective inertia at its base joint than a folded one); C(q,q̇)q̇ captures how the motion of one joint dynamically affects another through Coriolis and centrifugal effects; and G(q) is exactly the gravity-compensation torque referenced in feedforward control.
diagramCaption: A single pendulum-like arm under gravity: the torque needed at the joint has one term to accelerate the arm and a separate gravity-compensation term (mgL·cos θ) needed just to hold the current angle.
realWorldExamples: Selecting the correct motor for each joint of a robot arm by computing the worst-case torque needed across its full range of motion and expected payload — undersizing a motor here means the arm simply can't lift what it's supposed to.
The gravity-compensation feedforward term used in advanced robot arm controllers is computed directly from the G(q) part of the full dynamics equation.
Physics simulation environments (used for testing robot code before running it on real hardware) solve exactly these dynamics equations at every simulated timestep to produce realistic motion.
commonMisconceptions: "Kinematics and dynamics describe basically the same thing" — kinematics is purely geometric (position, velocity, no forces involved); dynamics is specifically about the forces and torques causing that motion, involving mass and inertia that kinematics never considers.

"Dynamics only matters for fast or heavy robots" — even a slow-moving, lightweight arm needs at least the gravity term accounted for, or it will droop or drift when merely trying to hold a fixed position.

"Newton-Euler and Lagrangian methods give different answers" — they are mathematically equivalent, always producing the same equations of motion for the same physical system; they differ only in derivation approach and computational efficiency, not in the physics they describe.
